_comment: Speeds are pixels per simulation tick; multiply by 60 for pixels per second.
A tile is 16 pixels, so 1.7 is about six and a half tiles a second.
Every enemy is slower than every class. That is the deal the whole fight
rests on: you can always disengage, so getting hit is a decision you made
rather than something the arena did to you. The binding number is the
Knight's 1.45 -- the slowest thing the player can be -- so nothing hostile
may exceed it, and a test enforces that against the slowest class rather
than against an average.
aggro is in pixels -- how far an enemy notices you from.
_class_comment: The five playable classes, in the order the character select shows them.
Anything with faction 'hero' is offered to the player, so this list is the
roster -- there is no second place to register a class.
They are separated by what they ask of you, not by a power level:
Knight    -- can you afford to commit? Slowest, toughest, hits hardest.
Rogue     -- can you stay in? Fragile, fastest, no swing costs anything.
Archer    -- can you keep the room between you? Ranged, average at all else.
Magician  -- can you find the gap? Long commitment, biggest single hit.
Priest    -- can you last? Middling everywhere, recovers twice as much.
heal_between_stages is the class's own dial, not a global one, and every
one of the five was measured separately rather than scaled from a single
number. Scaling was tried first and does not work: what a class needs back
between stages depends on how much damage it takes to clear one, and that
varies by more than its health pool does. On a median stage the Rogue and
the Archer spend about 17% of their bar, the Knight 27%, the Priest 30% --
so the Priest needs the largest heal as a fraction and the Rogue one of the
smallest, which is the opposite of what the health pools suggest.
That is also where the Priest's identity lives. Sixty-two of ninety-five is
two thirds of the bar back after every stage; nobody else clears half. It
is a run-level answer to a run-level problem, which is why the class looks
so ordinary on any single stage.
Rerun tools/balance.py --class all after touching any of these. They are
measured numbers and they do not survive being guessed at.

knight.name: Knight
_comment: The reference class -- the one the campaign is measured against, and the
default everywhere a class is not named. Most health, most damage, worst
mobility: the slowest roll on the longest cooldown, so disengaging is a
thing the Knight plans rather than a thing it does.

rogue.name: Rogue
_comment: Fastest body and fastest roll on the shortest cooldown. Eighty health is
about three hits from an act boss, so the mobility is not a luxury -- it
is the only defence the class has.

archer.name: Archer
_comment: Fights at the range the enemy archers want to, and wins that trade -- a
faster arrow and a much shorter windup. The catch is that a shot spends
itself on the first thing it touches, so the pillars that keep bowmen off
you also eat your damage, and a room full of rats closes the distance the
whole class depends on.

magician.name: Magician
_comment: The longest commitment of any class, on a body that cannot afford it.
Thirty-one ticks per bolt means every shot is a decision about the next
half second. Started at 75 health and lost six stages of the campaign
outright -- a class that commits for that long needs to survive being
wrong about it. The longest iframes in the game for the same reason.

priest.name: Priest
_comment: Unremarkable in a fight and hard to finish off across a campaign. Forty
health back between stages is more than twice anyone else, which makes a
badly cleared stage recoverable rather than a debt carried into the next
act. The class is a run-level answer to a run-level problem, which is why
it looks so ordinary on any single stage.

_advanced_comment: The ten promoted classes: two per starting class, chosen on clearing stage
20. Also faction 'hero', but 'promotes_from' keeps them out of
bestiary.hero_classes -- so they never appear on the character select, which
is laid out for five columns on a 384px screen. That one field is the whole
safety mechanism; without it these ten would join the roster and the select
screen at once.
They are NOT unmeasured any more. The balance grid is split at the fork:
the five starting classes are swept over stages 1-20 and these ten over
stages 21-40, one cell per class per stage. A branch that cannot clear act
VII fails the suite.
Deleting this section removes the feature. promotions_for() returns nothing,
the panel never opens, and no code has to be touched -- though the campaign
would then be twenty stages of content nobody can reach the far half of.
Each inherits its base's light and neutral attacks *by id*, so a promoted
class still opens a fight the way the one it grew out of did, and only the
top two slots are new. That inheritance is doing more work than it looks:
the light attack is most of what a fight is made of, so the hero's damage
per swing does not jump at the fork, which is what lets twenty more stages
sit behind it without a scaling layer under them. Radius, speed and the
dodge fields are inherited too: Entity.radius reads through to the type, so
a promotion that widened the body could leave the hero standing inside a
wall it was standing beside.
**heal_between_stages is no longer inert, and it had to be re-measured.**
It used to be: promotion happened on the way into the last stage and
nothing between stages ever happened again, so every branch simply
inherited the number and a test held it there. Twenty stages now follow the
fork and it pays out on every one of them.
Two of the five lines needed a bigger number for the second half and three
did not, which is the same shape the base classes' own heals have and for
the same reason -- what a class needs back between stages depends on how
much damage it takes to clear one, not on how much health it has:
knight  56 -> 84   1/6 runs at the inherited number, 6/6 at 84
rogue   38 -> 60   1/6 -> 4/6; the two seeds still lost are first-half
archer  30 -> 30   6/6 unchanged; fights at range and arrives healthy
magician 46 -> 46  every loss is in acts I-IV, so the dial does nothing
priest  62 -> 62   both losses are on stage 20, same reason
The rule that survived, and it is the point the old one was really making:
**the two branches of a class always share this number.** A tier may heal
more than the tier below it; a branch may never heal more than its twin.
'The healing one' is the obvious and wrong design for half of these -- the
Holy Priest and the Holy Knight would both collapse into it -- so a branch
earns 'outlasts it' from health, arc and knockback instead.
The heavies and the ultimates are still a first pass. The reference bot
plays light-only, and an advanced class's light is the one it inherited, so
promoting the bot did not widen what it can see. What is measured is each
branch's health and body against the late campaign; the twenty attacks are
not.

dark_knight.name: Dark Knight
_comment: Fifteen health traded for the two hardest attacks in the game. The Knight
is already the slowest thing the player can be, so this is not a class that
can retreat out of a mistake -- it is the branch that intends to finish the
Sovereign before the Sovereign finishes it.

holy_knight.name: Holy Knight
_comment: The largest health pool in the game and the hardest knockback, at the cost
of the damage the Dark Knight took. Twenty more health is about one and a
half more Lances from the Sovereign -- the branch that intends to still be
there at the end of a long fight.

assassin.name: Assassin
_comment: Four health above the Rogue and a great deal sharper. Both new attacks are
narrow enough to miss a body directly in front of you, which is the class
taken to its conclusion: everything it does asks whether you are in
exactly the right place.
**It was drafted at 78 -- two *below* the Rogue -- and that number was
written for a different game.** Trading health for burst is a fair deal
when the whole of the class's life is one fight against the Sovereign. It
is not a fair deal across twenty stages of attrition, and the measurement
was blunt about it: at 78 the Assassin failed six of the twenty late
stages, more than any other branch, while its twin at 88 failed two.
The Rogue line is the worst matchup in the game for acts V-VIII, and this
number is where that had to be paid. A five-damage dagger needs seven hits
to kill a revenant where the Knight's greatsword needs three, so the Rogue
spends more than twice as long inside reach of everything in the room. The
durability and composition levers were both spent before reaching for this
one -- class hp is last in the order for good reasons -- but no amount of
thinning a roster fixes a class that has to stand there twice as long.
Still the most fragile advanced class, which is the identity. It is no
longer the most fragile *body in the game*, which was never the intent.

shadow_rogue.name: Shadow Rogue
_comment: Eight more health, a roll one tick longer with one more invulnerable tick
in it, and the shortest dodge cooldown in the game at 18. The only branch
that changes a dodge number, because the roll is the Rogue's whole defence
and this is the branch that leans on it rather than on being somewhere
precise.
Drafted at 11 iframes on a 10-tick roll and rejected by test: invulnerable
for longer than the roll lasts makes the last frames of every dodge free,
and the correct play becomes rolling constantly rather than rolling at the
right moment. The gap between the two numbers is the point of both.

hunter.name: Hunter
_comment: Five more health and both new attacks pointed at one large body -- the
fastest projectile in the game and a five-shot fan tight enough that most
of it lands on a single target. The branch for out-shooting the Sovereign.

magic_archer.name: Magic Archer
_comment: The Archer's health, unchanged, and the widest attacks a hero has: the
fattest bolt in the game and nine shots across a hundred degrees. Answers
the Sovereign's Rain with a Rain, and answers the two grunts beside it at
the same time.

sage.name: Sage
_comment: Ten more health and a full-circle heavy. The Magician's standing problem
is that its 29-tick bolt is a long time to go uninterrupted on a body that
cannot afford to be; the Sage buys that time with health and with room
rather than by killing things faster.

wizard.name: Wizard
_comment: Five health lighter than the Magician, carrying the hardest projectile in
the game. Sixty-one ticks per Annihilate on a hundred-health body: the
branch that doubles down on the commitment the class was already built
around, rather than making it affordable.

battle_priest.name: Battle Priest
_comment: Ten more health and both new attacks in close. The Priest's kit buys space
it then does not use; this is the branch that stops buying it. Note the
heal is inherited and does nothing -- there is no stage after the one this
is chosen for.

holy_priest.name: Holy Priest
_comment: The obvious design for this class was 'heals more', and at this trigger
that is worth nothing at all. So its identity is the censer taken to its
limit instead: five more health, a full-circle ultimate and the second
hardest knockback in the game. The class that is never surrounded.

_enemy_comment: Anything with faction 'enemy'. Brains are code (game/ai.py), not data --
'chaser', 'charger', 'archer' and 'boss' are the four that exist, and two
different creatures sharing one is normal. The 'archer' brain in particular
describes a behaviour (keep your distance, need line of sight) rather than
a creature: both the bowman and the mage use it.
'level' is what a kill is worth, and nothing else reads it -- the sim has
no idea it exists. It runs 1 (rat) to 8 (sovereign) and it is ranked by how
much of a fight the thing is, not by its health: a brute has nearly four
times a bowman's hp and is worth twice as much, because most of that health
is time rather than danger. Heroes leave it at the default 1; nothing ever

grunt.name: Grunt
grunt._comment: Straightforward pressure. Walks at you, swings when close.

rat.name: Rat
_comment: Dies to one hit from anything and is barely slower than you, so it cannot
be outrun the way a grunt can -- it has to be dealt with. Individually
trivial and collectively the reason the second act is about crowd control
rather than about any one enemy.
Also the honest test of a ranged class: a rat closes the distance an
Archer or Magician is built around, and there are always more of them.

charger.name: Charger
_comment: Slow until it commits, then faster than you. Punishes standing in a line
with it. The long windup on 'gore' is the tell you dodge on.

brute.name: Brute
_comment: The slowest thing in the game that is not a boss, and the hardest hitting
thing that is not one either. Alone it is free damage -- you can walk away
from it indefinitely. The point of a brute is that it makes every other
enemy in the room more dangerous, because none of them let you spend the
time it takes to kill it.

bowman.name: Bowman
bowman._comment: Punishes standing still in the open. Backs away when you close.

mage.name: Mage
_comment: A bowman that stands further back and hurts much more. The hex is slow
enough to walk out of, so it costs you position rather than health -- and
position is what the third act keeps asking for.

_boss_comment: One boss ends each act: stages 5, 10, 15 and 20.
All four share the 'boss' brain, which is positional about its weapons --
weapons[0] is the sweep it uses up close, weapons[1] is the charge it uses
at mid range, weapons[2] is what it shoots from far away. Declare them in
any other order and it will telegraph one attack and land another. A test
enforces the ordering.
sprite_scale 2 is not decoration: render/hud.py decides what gets a boss
health bar by looking for it. A boss without it fights normally and shows
no bar.
Below half health every one of them stops pausing between attacks (see
game/ai.py). That is the whole phase system -- no new moves to learn at the
moment you are least able to learn them, just less room to breathe.
**On why the later bosses are not much tougher than the first.** There is
no progression in this game: the Knight that fights the Sovereign on stage
20 swings exactly the greatsword it had on stage 1. So health on a boss buys
fight *length* and nothing else -- and a fight twice as long against the same
moveset is not twice as interesting, it is the same fight with more chances
to make the one mistake that ends it.
This was measured rather than reasoned about. The Effigy started at 240 and
the Sovereign at 280, and both were unwinnable on every seed: not close,
not a tuning pass away -- the hero simply ran out of health partway down the
bar. What makes each of these harder than the Warden is the cadence, the
reach and the size of the arena, which is where a later boss should be
getting its difficulty from anyway.

boss.name: The Warden
_comment: End of act one, and the fight that teaches the pattern the other three
vary. Slower than anything else and much harder to kill, so it lasts long
enough for its three attacks to become something you read rather than
three things that happen to you.
aggro covers the whole arena -- there is no sneaking up on it, and no
corner it forgets about you in.

houndmaster.name: The Houndmaster
_comment: End of act two. Less health than the Warden and half again its speed --
the same three questions asked in a hurry. It closes the distance a ranged
class wants, and the shorter telegraphs mean the answers you learned on
stage five have to come faster rather than differently.

effigy.name: The Effigy
_comment: End of act three, and the opposite reading of the Warden: slower than
anything in the game, with the longest tells and the largest numbers.
Nothing it does is hard to see coming. The fight is long enough that the
question is whether you can keep answering correctly for two minutes, not
whether you can answer at all.

sovereign.name: The Sovereign
_comment: The end of act IV, and the last fight of the campaign's first half -- the
stage a class is promoted for clearing. Deliberately nothing new: the
same three attacks in the same three positions the Warden used fifteen
stages earlier, with every number raised and none of the room. Everything
the player learned still applies, which is the point of arriving at the
fork on it rather than on a fourth idea.
aggro of 700 covers any arena it could be placed in.

_acts_v_to_viii_comment: Acts V-VIII, stages 21-40, fought entirely as an advanced class.
Two ordinary enemies and four bosses. Two is a thin roster for four acts
and that is deliberate: an act introduces one idea, and the idea acts VII
and VIII introduce is the combination rather than a seventh creature. The
same shape act IV already had.
Both new enemies reuse a brain that exists. A fifth brain is code in
game/ai.py rather than content, and nothing here needs one -- what these
two do that nothing before them does is deny the two things the first
twenty stages let a player rely on: walking away from something durable,
and having twenty ticks to answer a charge.

revenant.name: Revenant
_comment: A brute's durability at a grunt's walking speed, which is the one
combination the first four acts never make. The brute is survivable
because you can leave it: it is slow enough to ignore for as long as you
like, and its danger is entirely the attention it costs. The revenant
cannot be left, so its health has to be spent rather than avoided.
Level 5 rather than 4: it is worth more than a brute because it is a
fight you do not get to decline.

stalker.name: Stalker
_comment: The charger's question asked from further out and answered in less time.
It commits from 210 where a charger commits from 150, and its tell is
26 ticks against the charger's 32.
It exists because of what promotion hands the player: a heavy and an
ultimate that are the longest commitments the hero has ever had. Without
something in the room that punishes spending one at the wrong moment,
the new kit is free damage and the second half of the campaign is easier
than the first.

herald.name: The Herald
_comment: End of act V, and the first fight after the fork. The Houndmaster's
shape -- quick body, short tells -- at the Sovereign's reach.
Chosen to be a pattern the player already knows, on purpose. The first
thing a newly promoted class meets should test the class, not teach a
fight: everything strange about this stage is supposed to be in the
player's own hands.

gaoler.name: The Gaoler
_comment: End of act VI. The Effigy's reading -- slowest body, longest telegraphs,
enormous reach -- pushed as far as it goes. A 50px chain across 240
degrees denies more floor than anything else in the game.
The slowest thing in the game and the hardest hitting. Both, because
neither alone is a fight at this point in a run.

choir.name: The Choir
_comment: End of act VII, and the least health of the four -- because it is the
one that has to be closed with, and a long fight at range is the failure
state rather than the fight.
Eleven shots across 130 degrees from 165 away. Standing off it is not a
strategy, and its arena is the most heavily pillared in the game so that
closing is a route rather than a sprint through a fan.

hollow_king.name: The Hollow King
_comment: Stage forty. The Sovereign's fight with every dial a shade further on --
more reach on the arc, more speed on the charge, ten shots instead of
nine -- and no new idea anywhere in it.
That is the same argument the Sovereign was built on and it is the
stronger one here, because this is the fight a player reaches with a
class they have been using for twenty stages. The last thing a campaign
should do is ask a question none of that prepared them for.
The most health of anything in the game, and only by twenty over the
Sovereign. Health on a boss buys length; it is a long fight because it
is the last one, not because length is what makes it hard.
